Our model row is one active identified customer in one calendar month. Frequency counts distinct eligible invoices. Invoice size is monthly eligible value divided by that count. We do not create zeros for months with no observed purchase. Missing customer IDs cannot receive a profile. Their eligible value remains visible in coverage and in the separate value table later.

KMeans assigns each point to the nearest center and updates centers to reduce squared distances. We choose three profiles in advance to keep the first description manageable. We do not claim three is optimal. Logarithms reduce the effect of large ranges. StandardScaler then prevents the GBP dimension from dominating invoice counts. Both are positive inputs and we retain large accounts. Our reference is simpler: two monthly-value percentiles estimated from training. We freeze those exact cutoffs for validation and test, so the later high-value fraction need not be exactly ten percent. Neither grouping has true class labels. They answer related descriptive questions.

Our supported conclusion is limited but useful. The model describes different purchasing patterns that a total-value rule mixes together. We can use that distinction to structure manual account review. If contribution alone is the question, the simple value rule may be enough. We have not estimated profit, future churn or campaign effects. The next improvement is recent data with verified identity links, comparable complete months and stakeholder review.
